Hi all,
Thanks for a very helpful call earlier today. Wanted to circle back with next steps based on our conversation.
1. As discussed, we'd love if you could please share with us the following items, by Thursday COB if possible (so we can
then get this back out to the members):
a- The top 3-5 questions/challenges within the DRG & anti-corruption portfolios that you would like the ACVFA working
group on this to focus on (for now at least). As a reminder you had already shared these questions in the initial draft
workplan, in case they remain similar.
b- Which specific members (full list here) you are most interested in working with, see as resources to your work, and/or
have relationships with.
2. As part of the upcoming public meeting in early December (date TBC this week), we will likely have 2 separate panels
on different priority issues (speakers would include ACVFA members, potential outside experts/leaders, local actors, etc.),
one of which will fall in the DRG/AC umbrella. MDM is an option but may be too contentious given the domestic context as
discussed -- are there other key issues within this space you would like to see highlighted in this first public meeting of the
committee? e.g. could be a sort of follow up to the UNGA bright spots event, or focus on tech, etc. Would love to hear
your thoughts, keeping in mind this is our first public meeting so the topic we choose will have added weight to it as an
Agency priority.
3. Regarding the IRC conversation specifically, we'd love to at some point connect relevant members with you Vera for a
briefing and bring them into the external stakeholder workstream once ready - let's keep in touch on timing for this as
things develop on both our ends but wouldn't be until later next month at least.
Thanks all very much and happy to discuss further at any time.
Best,
Sophia

USAID Information Resilience Council Launch. On October 3, USAID launched the Information
Resilience Council, an Agency-wide effort to develop solutions to dis/mis/mal information, and the impact
that weaponization of information, online hate speech and harassment have on democracy, all sectors of
development, and marginalized communities we serve all over the world. The Council will be led by Vera
Zakem of DDI/DRG, and include representation across all regional bureaus, as well as SEC, LPA, PPL,
DDI, BHA, GH, and M bureaus. The Council will convene AAs and DAAs roughly every 6-8 weeks; its core
work will be done by an Agency-wide working group, co-led by Meral Karan of DDI/DRG/Democracy,
Research, and Innovation, and Chris Runyan from the Africa Bureau front office. This working group will
focus on four lines of effort: optimizing USAID's programs in addressing mis/dis/malinformation; mitigating
operational risk to the Agency; communication and crisis response; and external engagement with the
technology sector, the interagency, our implementing partners, and Congress. Working group members will
subdivide to work on these key priorities. The next technical working group meeting will occur on Monday,
October 17.

Dear All,
We look forward to seeing you on Friday with DA Coleman, where we will discuss the Agency's
efforts to address disinformation. By way of background and for those who have not had a
chance to meet yet, I joined the DRG Center about three months ago as the Senior Advisor for
Tech and Democracy to help lead the Agency's efforts on digital democracy and combating
mis/dis/malinformation.
The purpose of this meeting will be to begin a discussion on how the Agency can better respond to
the ever growing threat of disinformation, and share more information about the "Information
Resilience Council" we are seeking to stand up. The Administrator has urged us to explore such a
Council as quickly as possible, and you will all receive an Action Memo for clearance in the next
week or two proposing its basic parameters. After initial introductions and opening remarks from
DA Coleman, I will provide an overview of key lines of effort and initiatives we hope this Council will
take on and coordinate across the Agency. We will then open the floor to your insights and
questions.
As this process gets underway, we would like to request your input on the following items:
• Please ID a senior level POC (either you or a DAA) to attend roughly bimonthly senior
level meetings like this one.
• Consider who in your Bureau at the technical level who can give a portion of their time
to participate in the working group that will carry out much of the Council's substantive
work.
• Consider what the main challenges to your bureau are related to this issue, and how an
optimal Council might meaningfully address them.
Thanks so much, and please let me know if you have any questions!
Vera

Summary of Conclusions Interagency Policy Committee
Meeting on Information Integrity and Resilience
USAID's Responses to the NSC:
(U//FOUO) Departments and agencies (D/As) will confirm in writing the primary office and
Deputy Assistant-level POC for all relevant information manipulation discussions, recognizing
that each primary lead may collaborate with different internal stakeholders on specific issues,
depending on the specific campaign theme, region, or actor involved. D/As can update that POC
formally in writing as necessary. If a D/A is unable to identify and confirm a primary lead office,
please provide a rationale in writing for NSC staff consideration.
• USAID DDI / DRG: Vera Zakem and Johnny Walsh
(U//FOUO) D/As reaffirmed the importance of a risk- calibrated approach to guide use of limited
resources to analyze and respond to specific information manipulation campaigns by foreign
state and non-state actors targeting U.S. national security interests. NSC staff reviewed NATO's
risk framework, and D/As provided feedback on its applicability to U.S. efforts to address
information manipulation and offered additional factors that could be taken into consideration,
including whether online dissemination of narratives is matched with offline activities. D/As will
review the NATO risk assessment framework and confirm support to pilot its use in analysis of
emerging information manipulation campaigns from foreign actors, providing as necessary
additional factors (with rationale) they believe should be incorporated into a risk assessment
framework. (Action: All, by July 22)
• USAID has a few recommendations regarding the NATO risk assessment framework-
• There should be a more nuanced approach to framing disinformation campaigns
through binary lenses in which hostile "external" actors or non-state actors are
targeting USG strategic interests. Political elites can also be co-opted or
independently gain disinformation tools which may also impact USG strategic
values and national security interests. The "disinformation industry" through
private companies or ad tech also has a role and can impact USG strategic
interests for financial gain.
• The NATO Risk Assessment only addresses mis/dis-information and does not
take into account factually accurate information that could be misrepresented to
discredit the US (such as discrediting our foreign policy in Ethiopia) or extreme
speech which could contribute to offline harm and even violence.

The risk ratings for Table 1 referencing 'reach' should not be used to tailor
response efforts. For example, the NATO risk assessments framework ranks
narratives that only appear on fringe outlets as green/"Low" for reach. Although
these types of narratives may not have a wide reach at the given time of
assessment, fringe outlets and websites are likely to be the source of conspiracy
theories and narratives that can trigger a wider and more viral response.
Therefore narratives with low reach or only resonating on fringe outlets should
not be underestimated. A green or "low" rating category may suggest a
correlation with a green or "low" response effort- whereas fringe outlets could
serve as early detection platforms and therefore may warrant more attention.
Additionally, the reach risk scale also neglects considerations around how
narratives are resonating in the information environment over a period of time.
• Table 2 of NATO's framework suggests a risk rating around USG policy
activities or capabilities. Generally USAID views this category in terms of risks
to USAID' s reputation (e.g. narratives where USAID is correlated with the CIA
or Tigray narratives). While this table is useful for addressing USG reputational
risks, it neglects disinformation campaigns that do not target US policies,
activities or capabilities (e.g. hate speech online that rises to the level of ethnic
violence around elections). While the former is a direct threat to the USG, the
later may have human security implications locally which can also impact US
foreign policy interests.
• (U//FOUO) D/As reaffirmed the importance of a risk-calibrated approach to guide use of
limited resources to analyze and respond to specific information manipulation campaigns
by foreign state and non-state actors targeting U.S. national security interests. NSC staff
reviewed NATO's risk framework, and D/As provided feedback on its applicability to
U.S. efforts to address information manipulation and offered additional factors that could
be taken into consideration, including whether online dissemination of narratives is
matched with offline activities. D/As will review the NATO risk assessment framework
and confirm support to pilot its use in analysis of emerging information manipulation
campaigns from foreign actors, providing as necessary additional factors (with rationale)
they believe should be incorporated into a risk assessment framework. (Action: All, by
July 22)
• USAID currently does not have the capabilities to identify disinformation risks
targeting the agency because USAID does not have social media analytics
capabilities monitoring for threats posed to USAID in the information
environment.

The NATO Risk framework suggests that information manipulation risks are only
a risk when they directly target the USG, our US foreign policy objectives and US
credibility. USAID's perception of risk is that information manipulation has
direct impacts, not just on reputational risk to USAID itself, to include our
Missions, staff and implementing partners- but directly impacts development
gains. Information manipulation has human security implications -both in kinetic
and non-kinetic environments, erodes democracies by delegitimizing elections or
institutions and the media sector, affects vaccination rates and trust in medical
providers and services, science integrity, beliefs in climate change, poses
challenges to academic institutions and economic growth.
• (U//FOUO) D/As will provide additional options to the draft catalog of near-term
response options available to D/As to respond to specific campaigns, or confirm the list
reflects the totality of current options. (Action: All, by July 22)
• While USAID is looking into capability to address near team response options,
USAID focuses on long term resilience to addressing information manipulation.
• (UI/FOUO) NSC staff will begin hosting a monthly sub-IPC-level call to sync on planned
public, congressional, and multilateral engagements related to information manipulation.
D/As are asked to provide to NSC staff their current topline press guidance on their work
on information manipulation. (Action: All, by July 22)
• USAID addresses information manipulation through four lines of effort (LOE) -
• This includes implementing programs that aim to build information
resilience among local communities, such as through our global health
programs which address rumors around COVID vaccinations or our
media programs that build media literacy skills.
• Our second LOE, is recognizing that our strategic and local messaging is
critical for conveying fact-based information about our USAID programs.
• Increasingly, USAID recognizes that there are operational risks to our
Missions, our staff and our implementing partners. USAID works in some
of the most challenging places in the world and often finds itself in
aggressive information environments in which USAID is becoming
targeted.
• Lastly, USAID values our interagency colleagues and recognizes the need
for a whole-of-government response to improve information ecosystems.
We aim to work closely with our implementing partners and civil societies
as well as the private sector.
• Mis/Dis/Mal-information is driven locally and requires context specific
solutions. USAID aims to build local capacity in this space by developing

independent and local skills to verify content- whether that means by building the
capacity to fact check, conduct social media analysis or through our media
literacy activities to enhance awareness of false content. The best solution to
addressing the information disorder problem is by placing the tools in the hands
of locals who have the linguistic skills and cultural understanding to detect when
content isn't authentically generated.
• USAID views that we need to take a whole-of-society approach to build
information resilience - which includes working with institutions of truth-telling
such as independent journalism, civil society organizers, forthright government
public communicators, academia, technology companies, advertisers and others
that provide fact-checking, investigations, media literacy that bolster societal
resilience and proactively blunt the impact of information manipulation. USAID
recognizes that the complex and fluid nature of mis-, dis- and malinformation
requires working beyond our traditional media partners to invest in: more diverse
multi-stakeholder working groups and initiatives, including participants from the
Global South and Big Tech, and pilots in social behavior change communication
and social impact entertainment that bring people together around shared norms
and values.
• USAID has had extensive experience working in the informational resilience
space. Much of our programming in this space has evolved from our work in the
media sector -which began over 30 years ago. We currently have media
programs in over 40 countries worldwide. We recognize that many of our
programs have had to pivot to address this emerging challenge and we need to
think more holistically about this problem.

FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY / SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED / USG INTERNAL
INFORMATION MEMO FOR ADMINISTRATOR POWER
Date:
July 11, 2022
Johnny Walsh, DDI/DAA, DDI's Center for Democracy, Human Rights, and
Governance (DDI/DRG)
Subject:
USAID Initial Response to Disinformation and Related Issues
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• DDI/DRG organized a full-day pan-USAID workshop on how we can better respond to
misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (sometimes abbreviated at USAID
as MDM). The exercise gathered roughly 50 participants, and reflected a shared judgment
that MDM has become a pervasive problem for USAID, the broader U.S. government
(USG), and the world. It poses significant risk to USAID and its staff, partners, and
programs, especially in the field.
• Key takeaways from the workshop included a shared perception that we are not set up
bureaucratically to programmatically or operationally respond well to MDM. Internally,
we need to share information, clarify roles, and tighten our operations. Externally, we
need more strategic and comprehensive partnerships with interagency leads on MDM, the
technology sector, and academia, among others.
• Moving forward, DDI/DRG will shepherd a process to better define the problem, produce
a framework document for our efforts moving forward, explore some form of
intra-agency entity on MDM, and use these tactics to strengthen USAID's response to the
needs identified above.
BACKGROUND:
On May 25th, DDI/DRG organized a strategic planning workshop with approximately 50
participants from each of the USAID Regional Bureaus, CPS, PPL, LPA, SEC, and DDI. Prior to
the workshop, DDI/DRG conducted an Agency-wide survey to gather feedback from
USAID/Washington and Missions, which solicited more than 100 responses. Below is a list of
key takeaways from those consultations:
• The need to share and learn from what different parts of the Agency are doing:
USAID requires Agency-wide guidance to address MDM. We need to systematically
share information on our programmatic and operational work streams across the Agency
(e.g. on security and reputational risk, strategic communications, cybersecurity, etc.).
USAID has considerable tools to counter MDM, given its global presence, local

partnerships, and work across diverse sectors, but the Agency must take a more
systematic approach to deploying those tools.
• The need to clarify roles, responsibilities, and response mechanisms within USAID:
MDM is a whole-of-Agency problem, but roles, responsibilities, and response
mechanisms are largely undefined — both within respective Missions, Bureaus, and
Independent Offices (M/B/IOs) and Agency-wide. While some M/B/IOs (e.g. DRG, OTI,
or GH) are tackling MDM through targeted programming and by measuring the
MDM-related impact of their programs, other M/B/IOs are less intentionally engaged on
MDM, and might benefit from institutional expertise on how MDM impacts their work
and best practices to address it. The respective roles of Legislative and Public Affairs
(LPA), Office of Security (SEC), Innovation, Technology, and Research Hub (ITR),
Office of Acquisition, and Assistance (OAA) and others are also important to define in
USAID's overall approach to combating MDM.
• The need to assess our operations in order to respond to reputational and security
risks: Information theft and manipulation affects USAID's reputation and security as
well as those of its staff and local partners. USAID has not adequately assessed
reputational and security risks to USAID mission staff and implementing partners
stemming from MDM campaigns, or the direct risks MDM may pose to its operations.
USAID also lacks communication guidance on how to best prepare to respond to targeted
MDM campaigns that affect its programs, staff, implementing partners, and civil society.
Further, there is no information sharing or reporting mechanism between USAID
missions and Washington Headquarters, creating gaps in information and awareness of
threats that could help reduce operational risks. A solution would entail clarifying
USAID's policies, organizational structures, training, resources, budget, contracting, and
personnel to document these instances - and more importantly, to better respond
• The need to strengthen interagency coordination: USAID could benefit from more
intentional interagency coordination both in DC and in the field. USAID employees
(leadership and working level) are not systematically made aware of or know how to
deploy the tools available across the USG that may help them in their response to MDM.
For example, the Global Engagement Center's (GEC) Insights Quantified (GEC-IQ)
platform offers analysis and social media analytics tools to track MDM campaigns.
Moving forward, USAID can better partner with the interagency in DC and in the field,
and through NSC processes like the "information integrity and resilience" and "sensitive
messaging" IPCs to strengthen the coordination. Our contribution will draw on our
programs and localized knowledge; we can also revisit applicable lessons learned from
the USG coordinating mechanisms for counterterrorism, countering violent extremism,
and atrocity prevention.
• The need for localized and contextual solutions to understand the information and
media environment: USAID's local knowledge and partnerships are a substantial
comparative advantage. We are well positioned to fill gaps that the interagency and the
tech sector often struggle to handle, especially by strengthening a society's resilience to
disinformation before any specific campaign takes root. For example in Georgia, USAID
2

is implementing a one of a kind "whole-of-society" program to address disinformation
and strengthening the resilience of the information environment at the local level by
providing targeted trainings to media and civil society, and working with local data
scientists, emerging technologists, religious figures, artists, and anthropologists
addressing MDM.
• The need to strengthen our relationship with the tech sector: USAID should
coordinate and expand partnerships with both established digital platforms and emerging
technology firms, particularly with an eye to places where these companies lack
significant local presence and operations to address MDM. Such partnerships could seek
to strengthen the information environment by supporting independent media, digital
literacy, and cyber hygiene training, as well as ways for local media, civil society,
democratic host-government counterparts, our missions, and implementing partners to
track, report and elevate MDM-related concerns more strategically and systematically.
• The need to elevate USAID's focus and capacities related to the cybersecurity of
programs: There is growing evidence that insufficient cybersecurity contributes to the
success of MDM campaigns directly harming our programs. In one recent instance, the
Nicaraguan government launched a two-year disinformation campaign against a local
civil society organization funded by USAID, to pave the way for a legal attack on the
partner and the media sector at large (lawfare) that resulted in prison sentences of 9-13
years for members of the local CSO. These campaigns are spread by coordinated troll
groups trained and funded by the government, as well as with technical support from
third country malign governments. During that disinformation campaign, the government
conducted cyberattacks on several media outlets that attempted to report on the
government's disinformation campaign. These incidents and broader trends strongly
indicate these types of attacks are more widespread and will continue to accelerate in
pace, scale, and sophistication. This could create an existential threat to USAID's ability
to ensure the security of local partners and to implement programs, especially in unstable
or otherwise closing spaces.
Elements of a Stronger USAID Response
At the workshop and in subsequent discussions, the Agency B/IO and DRG representatives have
identified several key things we as an Agency seek to accomplish en route to a more coordinated,
integrated, potent USAID capability to address MDM.
• Define the problem and our objectives. We will agree upon a definition that captures
the scope, scale, and distinctive challenge of disinformation at USAID. We will survey
USAID's existing efforts on MDM, identify gaps and opportunities, and develop a
manageable set of strategic objectives.
• Develop an interim framework document. This should address the challenge, provide
guidance to USAID Missions and B/IOs, and propose a manageable number of strategic
priorities on MDM, including identification of a few countries for cross-sector
interventions.
3

• Set up a USAID entity to lead on disinformation. This requires further thought, but we
are exploring a number of models for a Whole-of-Agency body to coordinate MDM
efforts. Key to this effort will be the ability to bring (depending on the situation) senior
leadership and working-level representatives from relevant regional and functional B/IOs
across the Agency, who can give a portion of their time to this challenge, to ensure we get
whole-of-agency, cross-sector representation. We envision this entity will be led by DRG,
but initially, will not be a full-time standing body or have its own budget. We want to
remain flexible as our needs to address this challenge evolve.
• Even such an internal body is sensitive right now because of the recent backlash
against DHS' "Disinformation Governance Board." To guard against any similar
backlash (against what would be a very different enterprise from DHS'), we will
work closely and transparently with the NSC, State, and others to ensure we are
avoiding all foreseeable pitfalls.
• Assess and Expand Programmatic Responses: We will catalog existing programs that
are addressing MDM, identify gaps and opportunities for innovation, and establish
mechanisms to share best practices. From this exercise we will develop strategic
objectives for USAID's overall programmatic response to this challenge.
• Reform USAID Operations: We will consult across the Agency, including with PPL,
LPA, SEC, ITR Cybersecurity, and HCTM, to identify needed operational changes, such
as best ways for the missions to respond to reputational, security risk, and employee
resilience. From this exercise we will establish clear strategic communication guidelines,
in collaboration with LPA. We will similarly identify MDM issues for our implementing
partners, and how we can respond.
• Strengthen External Partnerships: We will solidify external relationships with the tech
sector (social media and emerging technologies in Silicon Valley and in developing
countries where we serve), implementing partners, NGOs, and local institutions to elevate
and share MDM related challenges and best practices. One way that USAID can lead in
this arena is to support the formation of locally led independent coordination bodies,
inclusive of civil society, the tech sector, and relevant government stakeholders to elevate
and prioritize concerns, promote accountability, and facilitate cooperation.
NEXT STEPS:
I have asked Vera Zakem, our newly-arrived Senior Advisor for Tech and Democracy and a
broadly recognized expert on disinformation, to spearhead planning on this effort: defining the
problem, developing an interim framework document, planning for a cross-Agency entity to lead
on these issues, and mapping initial steps the Agency should take to begin reforming USAID
operations and strengthen external partnerships. Other experts across USAID will support Vera,
and we will work closely with interested bureaus at every turn. In the next month or two, we
4

will follow up with an Action Memo for your approval to launch some or all of these efforts in
earnest.

By Steven Lee Myers and Eileen Sullivan
July 6, 2022
WASHINGTON - The memo that reached the top of the Department of Homeland Security in September could not
have been clearer about its plan to create a board to monitor national security threats caused by the spread of
dangerous disinformation.
The department, it said, "should not attempt to be an all-purpose arbiter of truth in the public arena."
Yet when Secretary Alejandro N. Mayorkas announced the disinformation board in April, Republican lawmakers
and conservative commentators denounced it as exactly that, calling it an Orwellian attempt to stifle dissenting
views. So did some critics from the left, who questioned the powers that such an office might wield in the hands of
future Republican administrations.
Within weeks, the new board was dismantled — put on "pause," officially — undone in part by forces it was meant to
combat, including distortions of the board's intent and powers.
There is wide agreement across the federal government that coordinated disinformation campaigns threaten to
exacerbate public health emergencies, stoke ethnic and racial divisions and even undermine democracy itself. The
board's fate, however, has underscored how deeply partisan the issue has become in Washington, making it nearly
impossible to consider addressing the threat.
The failure to act, according to experts, has left openings for new waves of disinformation ahead of November's
midterm elections - and even for violence like the racist massacre at a Buffalo supermarket in May, which was
motivated by a baseless conspiracy theory that global forces aimed to "replace" white Americans with immigrants.
"I think we're in a really bleak situation here in this country," said Nina Jankowicz, who briefly served as the board's
director before resigning when the controversy boiled over.

Nicaraguan government launched a two-year disinformation campaign against a local
civil society organization funded by USAID, to pave the way for a legal attack on the
partner and the media sector at large (lawfare) that resulted in prison sentences of 9-13
years for members of the local CSO. These campaigns are spread by coordinated troll
groups trained and funded by the government, as well as with technical support from
third country malign governments. During that disinformation campaign, the government
conducted cyberattacks on several media outlets that attempted to report on the
government's disinformation campaign. These incidents and broader trends strongly
indicate these types of attacks are more widespread and will continue to accelerate in
pace, scale, and sophistication. This could create an existential threat to USAID's ability
to ensure the security of local partners and to implement programs, especially in unstable
or otherwise closing spaces.
Elements of a Stronger USAID Response
At the workshop and in subsequent discussions, the Agency B/IO and DRG representatives have
identified several key things we as an Agency seek to accomplish en route to a more coordinated,
integrated, potent USAID capability to address MDM.
• Define the problem and our objectives. We will agree upon a definition that captures
the scope, scale, and distinctive challenge of disinformation at USAID. We will survey
USAID's existing efforts on MDM, identify gaps and opportunities, and develop a
manageable set of strategic objectives.
• Develop an interim framework document. This should address the challenge, provide
guidance to USAID Missions and B/IOs, and propose a manageable number of strategic
priorities on MDM, including identification of a few countries for cross-sector
interventions.
3

• Set up a USAID entity to lead on disinformation. This requires further thought, but we
are exploring a number of models for a Whole-of-Agency body to coordinate MDM
efforts. Key to this effort will be the ability to bring (depending on the situation) senior
leadership and working-level representatives from relevant regional and functional B/IOs
across the Agency, who can give a portion of their time to this challenge, to ensure we get
whole-of-agency, cross-sector representation. We envision this entity will be led by DRG,
but initially, will not be a full-time standing body or have its own budget. We want to
remain flexible as our needs to address this challenge evolve.
• Even such an internal body is sensitive right now because of the recent backlash
against DHS' "Disinformation Governance Board." To guard against any similar
backlash (against what would be a very different enterprise from DHS'), we will
work closely and transparently with the NSC, State, and others to ensure we are
avoiding all foreseeable pitfalls.
• Assess and Expand Programmatic Responses: We will catalog existing programs that
are addressing MDM, identify gaps and opportunities for innovation, and establish
mechanisms to share best practices. From this exercise we will develop strategic
objectives for USAID's overall programmatic response to this challenge.
• Reform USAID Operations: We will consult across the Agency, including with PPL,
LPA, SEC, ITR Cybersecurity, and HCTM, to identify needed operational changes, such
as best ways for the missions to respond to reputational, security risk, and employee
resilience. From this exercise we will establish clear strategic communication guidelines,
in collaboration with LPA. We will similarly identify MDM issues for our implementing
partners, and how we can respond.
• Strengthen External Partnerships: We will solidify external relationships with the tech
sector (social media and emerging technologies in Silicon Valley and in developing
countries where we serve), implementing partners, NGOs, and local institutions to elevate
and share MDM related challenges and best practices. One way that USAID can lead in
this arena is to support the formation of locally led independent coordination bodies,
inclusive of civil society, the tech sector, and relevant government stakeholders to elevate
and prioritize concerns, promote accountability, and facilitate cooperation.
NEXT STEPS:
I have asked Vera Zakem, our newly-arrived Senior Advisor for Tech and Democracy and a
broadly recognized expert on disinformation, to spearhead planning on this effort: defining the
problem, developing an interim framework document, planning for a cross-Agency entity to lead
on these issues, and mapping initial steps the Agency should take to begin reforming USAID
operations and strengthen external partnerships. Other experts across USAID will support Vera,
and we will work closely with interested bureaus at every turn. In the next month or two, we
4

will follow up with an Action Memo for your approval to launch some or all of these efforts in
earnest.
